data.paper_title: The Cross-Section of Volatility and Expected Returns
data.selected_experiment: Table VI, Panel B: value-weighted quintile portfolios sorted on idiosyncratic volatility relative to the FF-3 model (1/0/1 strategy), July 1963 to December 2000

economic_rationale.value: The paper hypothesizes that firms with greater sensitivity to (negatively priced) aggregate volatility risk show larger idiosyncratic volatility relative to FF-3 and so earn lower returns; it then finds aggregate volatility exposure explains very little and calls the low returns of high-IVOL stocks a puzzle.

evidence.quote: Firms with greater sensitivities to aggregate volatility should therefore have larger idiosyncratic volatilities relative to the Fama-French model, everything else being equal.

universe_and_filters.value: NYSE, AMEX and NASDAQ stocks (implied by the NYSE-only robustness check); sample July 1963 to December 2000; no share-code, price, or minimum-observation filters stated for the idiosyncratic volatility sorts

evidence.quote: Excluding NASDAQ and AMEX has little effect on our results.

value: daily Fama-French factor returns (MKT, SMB, HML)

evidence.quote: we compute idiosyncratic volatilities from the regression (8) on daily data over an L month period

signal_formula_words.value: Idiosyncratic volatility: the standard deviation of the residuals from a regression of a stock's daily returns on the Fama-French three factors (MKT, SMB, HML), estimated over the past month of daily data.

evidence.quote: based on their level of idiosyncratic volatility computed using daily returns over the past month

signal_formula_symbols.value: r_it = alpha_i + beta_i^MKT MKT_t + beta_i^SMB SMB_t + beta_i^HML HML_t + eps_it (eq. 8); idiosyncratic volatility = sqrt(var(eps_it))

evidence.quote: rit = αi + βiM KT M KTt + βiSM BSM Bt + βiHM LHM Lt + εit. (8)
Portfolios are formed every month, based on volatility computed using daily data over the previous month.
We use a 1/0/1 strategy in both cases.
and we hold these value-weighted portfolios for 1 month.
The portfolios are rebalanced each month.

sort_rule_evidence.quote: in which we simply sort stocks into quintile portfolios

breakpoints.value: not stated (text implies equal-count quintiles of all sample stocks: quintile 5 contains 20% of the stocks)

evidence.quote: although quintile 5 contains 20% of the stocks sorted by idiosyncratic volatility
stocks with high idiosyncratic volatility have low average returns.
Stocks with high idiosyncratic volatility have abysmally low average returns.

weighting_evidence.quote: At time t, we construct value-weighted portfolios based on these idiosyncratic volatilities and hold these portfolios for N months.

expected_sign_evidence.quote: We ﬁnd that stocks with high idiosyncratic volatility have low average returns.

headline_result.value: Quintile 5 minus quintile 1 raw average return of -1.06% per month; FF-3 alpha difference of -1.31% per month (t-statistic -7.00)

evidence.quote: The difference in raw average returns between quintile portfolios 5 and 1 is -1.06% per month.

unresolved_details: Universe filters for the idiosyncratic volatility sorts (share codes, price screens, exchange coverage) are not stated in Section II; NYSE/AMEX/NASDAQ coverage is only implied.
Minimum number of daily observations required to estimate idiosyncratic volatility is not stated for Section II (Section I uses more than 17 daily observations for the beta_dVIX regression).
Whether regression (8) uses excess or raw stock returns is not stated.
Breakpoint universe (all stocks vs NYSE breakpoints) is not stated; equal-count quintiles across all stocks are only implied.
Exact definition of the formation month end (calendar month vs trading days) and the timing between formation and first return is not stated beyond the 1/0/1 description.
Treatment of delisting returns and missing returns is not stated.
Return convention: portfolio statistics are total, not excess, simple monthly returns.
